abstract: Connectome-constrained models are increasingly used to attribute behaviour to wiring, but their conclusions rest on modelling choices that the connectome does not fix. We independently replicated the rate model of the Drosophila nerve cord in which descending neuron DNg100 drives a walking rhythm generator (Pugliese et al., 2026), and asked which of its conclusions survive defensible alternatives to eleven such choices. Changed one at a time, 19 of 20 alternatives left the rhythm intact, including transfer of the wiring to a second connectome. Changed jointly, the rhythm survived in only 20 of 48 model variants when the descending drive was set by rules that do not look at the rhythm. A post hoc sweep of the drive separated two causes. In 12 of the 28 failures a rhythm existed at another drive, in 11 of them a higher one: the published drive lies at the lower edge of the rhythmic range. The other failures concentrated where larger networks met two- or threefold heterogeneity of intrinsic parameters, an interaction that one-at-a-time tests cannot show. In the 31 variants with a rhythm at a common drive of the sweep, the two excitatory interneurons remained necessary (30 of 31) and the inhibitory interneuron dispensable (29 of 31). The rhythm stayed rare among degree-preserving rewired networks when their drive was swept as well, and left-right coupling in the model was weak. The operating point is a modelling choice in its own right, and what a connectome model "produces" should be reported across it.
